title: Impact of British Rule on India: Economic, Social and Cultural (1757–1857)
summary: After Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India in 1498, the Portuguese, Dutch, French and English came to trade and to spread Christianity. Britain's Industrial Revolution needed raw materials and markets, and the decline of the Mughal Empire gave the British a chance to gain power through wars, forced treaties, annexations and alliances. Land revenue policies, commercial crops, monopoly of trade, railways and English education helped them establish and continue their rule.

The East India Company was set up in 1600. Its first factory was at Surat (1613); in 1615 Sir Thomas Roe got Jahangir's permission for factories at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach; Fort St. George was built at Madras; and in 1696 three villages in Bengal were developed into Calcutta (Kolkata) with Fort William.

The Battle of Plassey (1757), after which Mir Jafar was made Nawab of Bengal, and the Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764) against Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Awadh and Shah Alam II, laid the base of British power. Mysore under Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan fought four wars; Tipu died in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799). The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19) ended Peshwa rule. After Maharaja Ranjit Singh's death, the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845, 1849) led Dalhousie to annex Punjab.

Under the Doctrine of Lapse, a protected state whose ruler died without a natural heir was annexed: Satara (1848), Sambalpur, Udaipur, Nagpur, Jhansi (1854) and Awadh (1856). Under the Subsidiary Alliance, Indian states disbanded their armies, kept British troops and gave up control of foreign affairs in return for protection.

In 1813 the Company's trade monopoly ended and India became an economic colony of industrial England. British machine-made cloth entered India duty-free while Indian goods were taxed heavily, so Indian handlooms collapsed (de-industrialisation): India changed from an exporter of cloth to an exporter of raw cotton and importer of British cloth, and weavers became farm labourers.

Land revenue: the Permanent Settlement (Lord Cornwallis, 1793, Bengal and Bihar) made zamindars hereditary owners who paid a fixed sum; if they failed, their land was sold. The new zamindars became allies of the British. The Mahalwari Settlement (1822; North-Western Provinces, Punjab, Ganga valley, parts of Central India) assessed a mahal (village or group of villages) jointly. The Ryotwari Settlement (Bombay and Madras) taxed the individual cultivator directly. All demanded very high revenue.

Commercialisation of agriculture: tea, coffee, indigo, opium, cotton, jute, sugarcane and oilseeds were grown for British needs. Farmers were forced to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land, which made the soil infertile. Food production fell and famines followed. Peasants borrowed from moneylenders, who used false accounts and high interest, and their land passed to the money-lending class. A new middle class of agents, new zamindars and English-educated professionals arose. Wealth was drained to Britain.

Railways connected raw-material areas with ports; British investors got a guaranteed 5% profit and free land. The first railway was the Red Hill line in Madras (1837, for granite); the first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane (1853). Dalhousie opened the first telegraph line (Calcutta–Agra) and postal service. Railways also, unintentionally, brought people and ideas together.

Practices such as sati, child marriage, female infanticide and untouchability were common. Western ideas of liberty and equality inspired reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Sir Syed Ahmad Khan. Laws: sati banned (1829, Lord Bentinck); Widow Remarriage Act (1856); inter-caste marriages allowed (1872); Sharda Act (1929) against child marriage.

Education policy: English was taught to create cheap, loyal clerks and a market for British goods. The Charter Act of 1813 gave Rs 1 lakh for education; Wood's Despatch (1854) led to Departments of Education and universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857). Mass education was ignored, but English became the link language, spread ideas of liberty, democracy and nationalism (Locke, Mill, Rousseau; Mazzini and Garibaldi became heroes). Orientalists set up the Calcutta Madrasa (Warren Hastings, 1781), the Asiatic Society of Bengal (William Jones, 1784), the Sanskrit College at Banaras (Jonathan Duncan, 1794) and Fort William College (Wellesley, 1800).
Administration and courts: Indians were kept out of high posts; codified laws and civil and criminal courts were introduced, but justice was costly and discriminated between Europeans and Indians.

Heavy taxes, eviction and frequent famines led to revolts of Sanyasis and Fakirs, Poligars, Mappilas, Jats, Kolis, Bhils and Santhals. The Revolt of 1857 united people of different backgrounds, ended Company rule and gave rise to nationalism; afterwards the British followed a policy of Divide and Rule. Railways, English language, civil services, clothes and food habits remain as legacies of British rule.

objective: Fill in the blanks: (a) In 1822 the British introduced the ____ land revenue system in the North-Western Provinces, Punjab, the Ganga valley and parts of Central India. (b) The first railway line, the Red Hill line of Madras, opened in 1837 and was used to carry ____.

Complete the sentences: (I) England succeeded in controlling trade with India and established the East India Company in ____. (II) In 1696 the Company developed three villages into a city in Bengal and named it ____.
Fill in the blanks: Under the ____ Alliance, Indian states had to disband their armies and keep British troops; under the Doctrine of ____ states without a natural heir were annexed.

vsa: Explain any two features of the Permanent Settlement.

(1) Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793 in Bengal and Bihar, it made zamindars hereditary owners of land who deposited a fixed amount of revenue in the treasury. (2) If a zamindar failed to pay on time his land was sold; the British got a fixed income and the zamindars became their political allies.
Why did the British invest in improving transport in India? Give two reasons.

(1) Railways connected the raw-material-producing areas with the ports so cotton, indigo and other crops could be exported easily. (2) They carried British finished goods to markets all over India; British investors also got a guaranteed 5% profit on railway capital.

or: Why did the British create a class of English-educated Indians? Give two reasons.

(1) English-educated Indians could work as clerks on low wages, reducing the cost of administration. (2) The British hoped this class would be loyal, appreciate British culture, spread it to others and increase the market for British goods, strengthening British rule.

vsa: Explain any two reasons why the class of moneylenders grew during British rule.

(1) The time-bound and excessive revenue demands forced peasants to borrow from moneylenders. (2) The new legal system helped moneylenders, who charged high interest and used false accounts; when peasants could not repay, their land passed to them.
Why did the British pressurise Indian farmers to cultivate indigo?
Indigo was needed in England as a dye for cloth produced in British mills. Farmers were forced to grow it on 3/20th of their land and sell it on terms dictated by British planters.
Mention two legal measures which helped improve the status of women in British India.
(1) Sati was banned in 1829 by Lord Bentinck. (2) The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 allowed widows to remarry. (The Sharda Act of 1929 also prevented child marriage.)
sa: How did the British use political power, trade policies and education to strengthen their control over India? Analyse.

(1) Political power: through wars (Plassey, Buxar), the Subsidiary Alliance and the Doctrine of Lapse they annexed Indian states and ruled directly. (2) Trade policies: they monopolised trade, bought raw materials cheap, let British goods in duty-free and taxed Indian goods, ruining Indian industry and making India a supplier of raw materials and a market. (3) Education: English education produced cheap, loyal clerks and a class that admired British culture and helped run the administration.
Explain the impact of British trade on the Indian handloom weaving industry.

British machine-made cloth was cheap and entered India without duty, while Indian handicrafts were taxed heavily and Britain put protective tariffs on Indian textiles. India changed from an exporter of cloth to an exporter of raw cotton and importer of British cloth. Handloom weaving collapsed (de-industrialisation), weavers became unemployed and moved to villages as farm labourers, increasing pressure on agriculture.
Why did the British pressurise the cultivation of indigo in India? Explain the reasons for the discontent of the farmers.

Indigo was needed as a dye for British textile mills. Discontent: (1) farmers were forced to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land; (2) they had to sell it at prices dictated by the planters; (3) indigo cultivation made the land infertile for some years and reduced land for food crops.
Explain the impact of the British education policy on India.

(1) English was introduced to create cheap clerks and a loyal class; the Charter Act of 1813 and Wood's Despatch (1854) led to English schools and universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857). (2) Mass and elementary education was neglected; education became a monopoly of the rich and city dwellers. (3) But English became a link language and Western ideas of liberty, equality and democracy spread, producing reformers and nationalists.
Distinguish between the Permanent Settlement and the Mahalwari Settlement.

Permanent Settlement (1793, Bengal and Bihar): the zamindar was made the hereditary owner and paid a fixed revenue; his land was sold if he failed to pay. Mahalwari Settlement (1822, North-Western Provinces, Punjab, Ganga valley): revenue was assessed on the produce of a mahal (village or group of villages) and all its proprietors were jointly responsible. Under both, revenue demands were very high and peasants suffered.
Why did the British seek to restrict the development of India? Explain.

(1) Britain wanted India as a source of cheap raw materials for its factories. (2) It wanted India as a market for its finished goods, so Indian industries were not allowed to compete. (3) Heavy duties on Indian goods and free entry for British goods protected British industry. These policies drained India's wealth and kept it poor.
la: Explain the economic impact of British rule on India in six points.

(1) De-industrialisation: cheap, duty-free British cloth ruined Indian handlooms and other crafts. (2) India became an exporter of raw materials and importer of finished goods. (3) The Permanent, Mahalwari and Ryotwari settlements imposed very high land revenue, impoverishing peasants. (4) Commercialisation of agriculture (indigo, opium, cotton, tea) reduced food crops and led to famines. (5) Peasants fell into debt and lost land to moneylenders; a new middle class of agents and zamindars arose. (6) There was an enormous drain of wealth to Britain through profits, salaries and pensions; railways were built mainly to serve British trade.
Highlight the impact of the British on Indian society and culture in the 19th century.

(1) Western ideas of liberty, equality and human rights reached India and inspired reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy. (2) Laws were passed against sati (1829), for widow remarriage (1856), inter-caste marriage (1872) and against child marriage (Sharda Act 1929). (3) English education created a new middle class and a link language. (4) Orientalists founded the Asiatic Society and Fort William College, reviving interest in India's past. (5) The press, literature and theatre spread national consciousness. (6) But Indians were excluded from high posts, justice was costly and discriminatory, and the Divide and Rule policy harmed Hindu–Muslim relations.
